quotes.t: Since the Cabalist wise men believe that many of the ancient fathers died in this kind of rapture of the intellect, you will find the Cabalists saying that those fathers died of binsica which in our language means death from …

rel.basis: Allen reports Pico naming Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron and Mary as dying binsica, death by a kiss, the same list Wirszubski traces to Recanati's text.

Allen reports Pico citing Solomon's 'kiss me' verse for the death of the kiss; Wirszubski identifies this same assumption as the link Pico's Commento draws between the Symposium and the Song of Solomon.

Allen quotes the Commento gloss that man passing to intellectual existence is transformed into an angel as the Cabalists say Enoch was transformed into Metatron, the angel of divinity; Wirszubski quotes the same Commento sentence (Enoch in Matatron, angelo della divinita).
Both state that the Commento cites the Cabalists' teaching that Enoch was transformed into Metatron, angel of divinity, as the pattern for a man's transformation into an angel.
Both read the Commento's gloss on love and death as saying that passing to the intellect away from the corporeal transforms man into an angel, and that this was Enoch's fate.
Both quote or paraphrase the same Commento gloss: union with intelligible Beauty/heavenly love transforms a man into an angel, as the Cabalists say Enoch became Metatron.

judged.justification: Ties the Death of the Kiss to the Enoch-Metatron transformation in the Commento.

quotes.t: To attain such a gift, the soul separates from the body, but, even more importantly, the body drops away entirely from the soul. We cease to be humans and become angels - the cherubim and seraphim of Ezekiel's great vision.

rel.basis: Allen's account that the kiss-death makes us cease to be human and become the cherubim and seraphim of Ezekiel's vision explains what Howlett calls the soul's emancipation from materiality in the Kabbalistic trope of the kiss of death.

open.t: Whether Pico intends the first or the second death for Orpheus is left open.

rel.basis: Howlett's quotation of Pico resting at the sixth step, barred from the seventh sabbath of full union with the First Father, answers Allen's open question about whether Pico means Orpheus should have died the 'second death': on Howlett's reading even the highest death-of-the-kiss stops short of unio mystica with the One itself.

bears.note: Pico's denial that God loves us is directed at Ficino's doctrine of reciprocation.

rel.basis: Howlett quotes Pico's Commentary that love is 'not love which might be in Him, as Marsilio believes, because then there would be imperfection in Him'; Allen independently reports that Pico's denial that God loves us was 'to shock the reader, or at least to refute Ficino, who is specifically cited as believing, incorrectly, that God loves us' -- the same passage and the same identification of its target.

judged.justification: Identifies a concrete doctrinal target of Pico's anti-Ficinian polemic.

bears.note: Contrast: Pico keys the Commento to being, Ficino to unity.
Pico is indebted to Platonic Theology III.

judged.justification: Places the being/unity split, later central to De ente et uno, already in the Commento.

rel.basis: Howlett reports Lohr's finding that the causal/formal being distinction Pico 'consistently makes' has a Thomist origin; Allen's independent description of the Commento's opening move, distinguishing 'causal, formal and participated being' and defining God as 'cause of being ... rather than as being or intellect per se', supplies the very triad whose Thomist genealogy Lohr traces.

quotes.t: This leads Pico from the onset to challenge the reaction of amazement by "un gran platonico" (clearly Ficino) to a passage in Plotinus's Enneads (5.6.3 or 6.7.37) in which God is said to understand nothing and to castigate him for …

bears.note: Pico's opening polemic against Ficino's reading of Plotinus on God's understanding.

rel.basis: Allen reports Pico challenging 'a great Platonist' (identified as Ficino) amazed that Plotinus said God 'understands nothing', explaining the attribute exists in God 'in its causal not formal being'; Howlett independently reports the identical point: Pico says God is 'being itself' whereas 'the Plotinian One is considered, by Plotinus and Ficino, to be above being' -- the same episode and the same causal/formal distinction as its resolution.

bears.note: Allen defends Ficino against Pico's charge of misunderstanding.

Angel as composite of potency and act, an Aristotelian gloss on the Platonic second hypostasis.

quotes.t: But Mind, identified hypostatically with Saturn, nonetheless has three functions - a Saturnian contemplation of (Ficino was to call this, more logically, a Uranian regarding of) things higher than itself (but such can only be God); a Saturnian contemplation "that …

bears.note: Allen notes Ficino's later relabelling of Pico's Saturnian functions as Uranian and self-regarding.

open.t: Allen holds the Commento's distribution of potency and act across Mind's three functions incoherent; the source reading may differ.

quotes.t: Moreover, since Mind is the first one-and-many and exists both as the first angel and as the plenitude of the Ideas, it is the first unitary composite and therefore the first beautiful thing: not so much the absolute, exemplary unique …

bears.note: Allen says Ficino would consistently call this composite beauty the splendor of the Ideas.

judged.justification: Centres the Poros/Penia lemmata as the seat of Pico's angelic-Mind doctrine.

rel.basis: Both state, from the Commento, that Pico locates causal being in God, formal being in Mind, and participated being in the rational soul, against a simpler Ficinian single locus of being in the angelic mind.
Howlett's quotation of the Commento's causal-being-in-divinity, formal-being-in-angelic-nature distinction restates the same triad of being Allen describes from the same work.

quotes.t: Pico takes Plato's description of Porus as drunk with nectar to signify "the sheer multiplicity of the Ideas" (l'affluenzia universale d'esse idee), presumably the Ideas of all the other things that were there in Mind, or possibly all the Ideas …

For, he concludes 2.13 with the argument that "although the Ideas of other things existed in the Angelic Mind, Plato does not say that they were welcomed to the banquet, because the gift of immortality was not granted to them."

judged.justification: Shows convergence, not only quarrel, between Pico and Ficino on angelic Mind.

quotes.t: Pico adduces the Orphic verses in 2.14 and 2.22 and observes that Mind could "rightly be called a chaos" when it was first filled with all the Ideas and the Ideas were still "imperfect, indistinct as it were, and confused."

Since the Ideas can be perfected only when they are separated from what is alien to them, separated in effect from the as yet unformed chaos of Mind and returned to their source in the One, Mind must itself revert …

judged.justification: The return of angelic Mind to God as a complete circle: the metaphysical frame for the Death of the Kiss.
